summary.text: For \(M\) divisible by \(p\) and \(e=v_p(M)\), the numerator is split according as \(p\mid k\), and its difference from \(p\) times the numerator at \(M/p\) is shown divisible by \(p^{4e}\); dividing by \(M\) then leaves \(p^{3e}\).  The \(p\nmid k\) part is handled by extracting \(M^3\) and inducting over \(p\)-adic blocks using vanishing inverse-square unit sums and a peeled binomial-ratio congruence, while the \(p\mid k\) part uses a refined Jacobsthal congruence from paired product factors together with Kummer carry bounds; finally \(e=v_p(np^r)\ge r\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 C_{N,k}:=\binom{N+k-1}{N-1}=\binom{N+k-1}{k}
\]
for \(N\geq1\), and put
\[
 b(N):=\sum_{k=0}^{N}(N+2k)C_{N,k}^{3}.
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is \(a(N)=b(N)/N\). We shall prove the stronger intermediate assertion
\[
 p^{4v_p(M)}\mid b(M)-p\,b(M/p)                                      \tag{1}
\]
whenever \(p\geq5\) is prime, \(M\geq1\), and \(p\mid M\). Here and below \(v_p(x)\) denotes the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\).

We use congruences and divisibility in the ring of \(p\)-adic integers. Every ordinary integer not divisible by \(p\) is a unit there, so expressions such as \(i^{-1}\) are legitimate whenever \(p\nmid i\). A divisibility statement by a power of \(p\) in this ring is equivalent to the corresponding ordinary integer divisibility when the quantity involved is an integer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Inverse-square block sums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We first establish the harmonic-sum fact used throughout the proof. For every \(s\geq1\),
\[
 \sum_{\substack{x\bmod p^s\\p\nmid x}}x^{-2}\equiv0\pmod{p^s}.       \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, in the ring \(\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z\), multiplication by \(2\) permutes the units. Hence, if
\(T=\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z)^\times}x^2\), then
\[
 T=\sum_x(2x)^2=4T,
\]
so \(3T=0\). Since \(p\geq5\), \(3\) is a unit modulo \(p^s\), and therefore \(T=0\). Inversion also permutes the units, giving (2).

The summand in (2), regarded as a function of an integer, is periodic modulo \(p^s\). Consequently every interval of \(p^s\) consecutive integers gives the same sum. Thus, for every integer \(A\),
\[
 \sum_{\substack{A\leq x<A+p^s\\p\nmid x}}x^{-2}\equiv0\pmod{p^s}.   \tag{3}
\]
Define the corresponding \(p\)-adic block sum
\[
 W_s(l):=\sum_{\substack{p^sl\leq x<p^s(l+1)\\p\nmid x}}x^{-2}.
\]
Then
\[
 p^s\mid W_s(l),                                                       \tag{4}
\]
and merging \(p\) consecutive blocks gives
\[
 \sum_{\sigma=0}^{p-1}W_s(p\mu+\sigma)=W_{s+1}(\mu).                 \tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Peeling binomial products
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We require a product identity that removes the factors divisible by \(p\). For integers \(a,l\geq0\),
\[
 \binom{ap+l}{l}
 \prod_{i=1}^{l}\begin{cases}1,&p\mid i,\\ i,&p\nmid i,
 \end{cases}
 =
 \binom{a+\lfloor l/p\rfloor}{\lfloor l/p\rfloor}
 \prod_{i=1}^{l}\begin{cases}1,&p\mid i,\\ ap+i,&p\nmid i.
 \end{cases}                                                        \tag{6}
\]
This follows directly from
\( inom{ap+l}{l}=\prod_{i=1}^l(ap+i)/i\): among the factors with \(p\mid i\), write \(i=pj\) and cancel the common factor \(p\); their product is precisely the lower-level binomial coefficient. Equivalently, (6) can be proved by induction on \(l\), separating the cases \(p\mid l\) and \(p\nmid l\).

We also need the following no-carry observation. If \(0\leq l<p^r\), then
\[
 p\nmid\binom{cp^r+l}{l}.                                             \tag{7}
\]
In base \(p\), adding \(l\) to \(cp^r\) creates no carry among the last \(r\) digits, so Kummer's theorem gives (7). One may also prove it recursively from Lucas' congruence:
\[
 \binom{cp^r+l}{l}\equiv
 \binom{cp^{r-1}+\lfloor l/p\rfloor}{\lfloor l/p\rfloor}
 \binom{l\bmod p}{l\bmod p}\pmod p,
\]
ending at \(1\). Thus every binomial coefficient in (7) is a \(p\)-adic unit.

For fixed nonnegative integers \(c,w,r,l\), define
\[
 Q_{r,l}(c,w):=
 \frac{\binom{(c+w)p^r+l}{l}}{\binom{cp^r+l}{l}}
 \quad(0\leq l<p^r).                                                  \tag{8}
\]
The denominator is a unit by (7). Applying (6) to numerator and denominator shows that, for \(l<p^{r+1}\),
\[
 Q_{r+1,l}(c,w)\equiv Q_{r,\lfloor l/p\rfloor}(c,w)
       \pmod{p^{r+1}}.                                                 \tag{9}
\]
To see the modulus explicitly, after peeling, the extra product is over \(p\nmid i\), and its numerator and denominator factors are
\((c+w)p^{r+1}+i\) and \(cp^{r+1}+i\). Their difference is \(wp^{r+1}\), while both are units. Hence every extra ratio is \(1\pmod{p^{r+1}}\), and so is their product.

Now define
\[
 \Phi_r^{(s)}(c,w):=
 \sum_{l=0}^{p^r-1}Q_{r,l}(c,w)^3W_s(l).
\]
We claim
\[
 p^{r+s}\mid\Phi_r^{(s)}(c,w)\qquad(s\geq1).                          \tag{10}
\]
This is proved by induction on \(r\). For \(r=0\), the sum has only \(l=0\), \(Q_{0,0}=1\), and (10) is exactly (4). For the induction step write \(l=p\mu+\sigma\), with \(0\leq\mu<p^r\), \(0\leq\sigma<p\). By (9),
\[
 Q_{r+1,p\mu+\sigma}^3\equiv Q_{r,\mu}^3\pmod{p^{r+1}}.
\]
The difference of the cubes is divisible by \(p^{r+1}\), while \(W_s(p\mu+\sigma)\) is divisible by \(p^s\). Therefore
\[
 \Phi_{r+1}^{(s)}(c,w)\equiv
 \sum_{\mu=0}^{p^r-1}Q_{r,\mu}^3
       \sum_{\sigma=0}^{p-1}W_s(p\mu+\sigma)
 \pmod{p^{r+s+1}}.
\]
By (5), the right side is \(\Phi_r^{(s+1)}(c,w)\), which is divisible by \(p^{r+s+1}\) by induction. This proves (10).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The terms whose index is not divisible by \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write
\[
 M=p^eu,\qquad e=v_p(M)\geq1,\qquad p\nmid u.
\]
Let
\[
 S_0:=\sum_{\substack{0\leq k\leq M\\p\nmid k}}
 (M+2k)C_{M,k}^3.
\]
We prove
\[
 p^{4e}\mid S_0.                                                       \tag{11}
\]

For \(k\geq1\), the elementary identity
\[
 k\binom{M+k-1}{k}=M\binom{M+k-1}{k-1}                               \tag{12}
\]
gives, because \(k\) is a unit,
\[
 C_{M,k}=M k^{-1}\delta_k,
 \qquad \delta_k:=\binom{M+k-1}{k-1}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 S_0=M^3G,
\quad
 G:=\sum_{\substack{0\leq k\leq M\\p\nmid k}}
       (M+2k)\delta_k^3k^{-3}.                                       \tag{13}
\]
It is therefore enough to prove \(p^e\mid G\).

Partition \(0\leq k<M=p^eu\) into blocks
\[
 k=p^eK+L,\qquad 0\leq K<u,
 \quad 0\leq L<p^e,
\]
retaining only \(p\nmid L\). (The endpoint \(k=M\) is divisible by \(p\), so it contributes nothing.) We show that each block sum in (13) is divisible by \(p^e\).

Introduce
\[
 H_k:=2\delta_k^3k^{-2}.
\]
Then
\[
 (M+2k)\delta_k^3k^{-3}-H_k=M\delta_k^3k^{-3},
\]
which is divisible by \(p^e\). Thus it remains to show that the sum of the \(H_k\)'s over each block is divisible by \(p^e\).

Put \(r=e-1\), and write uniquely
\[
 L=p\lambda+\rho,
 \quad 0\leq\lambda<p^r,
 \quad 0\leq\rho<p,
 \quad p\nmid\rho.
\]
A one-level scale descent obtained from (6) says that, for \(B\leq A\), \(t\geq1\), and \(x\geq0\),
\[
 \binom{Ap^t+x}{Bp^t+x}
 \equiv
 \binom{Ap^{t-1}+\lfloor x/p\rfloor}
       {Bp^{t-1}+\lfloor x/p\rfloor}
 \pmod{p^t}.                                                         \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, in the peeled product all nonmultiples-of-\(p\) numerator factors differ from the corresponding denominator factors by \((A-B)p^t\); the denominator product is a unit, so it can be cancelled.

Apply (14), first with \(x=p\lambda+\rho-1\), and then with \(x=0\). Combining the resulting congruences with
\[
 \binom{(u+K)p^r+\lambda}{Kp^r+\lambda}
 \binom{Kp^r+\lambda}{\lambda}
 =
 \binom{(u+K)p^r+\lambda}{\lambda}
 \binom{(u+K)p^r}{Kp^r},                                             \tag{15}
\]
we obtain
\[
 \delta_{p^eK+p\lambda+\rho}
 \equiv
 \binom{(u+K)p^e}{Kp^e}\,Q_{r,\lambda}(K,u)
 \pmod{p^e}.                                                         \tag{16}
\]
The denominator \(\binom{Kp^r+\lambda}{\lambda}\) used in passing from (15) to (16) is a unit by (7). Also
\[
 (p^eK+p\lambda+\rho)^{-2}
 \equiv(p\lambda+\rho)^{-2}\pmod{p^e}.                              \tag{17}
\]
Cubing (16), multiplying by (17), and summing gives
\[
 \sum_{\substack{0\leq L<p^e\\p\nmid L}}H_{p^eK+L}
 \equiv
 2\binom{(u+K)p^e}{Kp^e}^{3}
 \sum_{\lambda=0}^{p^r-1}Q_{r,\lambda}(K,u)^3
 \sum_{\substack{0\leq\rho<p\\p\nmid\rho}}
       (p\lambda+\rho)^{-2}
 \pmod{p^e}.
\]
The double sum is exactly \(\Phi_r^{(1)}(K,u)\), and (10) says it is divisible by \(p^{r+1}=p^e\). Hence every block sum is divisible by \(p^e\). From (13), \(M^3\) supplies another \(p^{3e}\), proving (11).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. A refined Jacobsthal congruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We next prove the estimate needed for the terms with index divisible by \(p\). The key statement is: for \(A,B\geq1\), if
\[
 v_p(B)\leq1+v_p(A)+v_p(A+B),                                        \tag{18}
\]
then, with \(\gamma=v_p\binom{A+B}{B}\),
\[
 p^{\gamma+3+v_p(A+B)+v_p(B)+v_p(A)}
 \mid
 \binom{p(A+B)}{pB}-\binom{A+B}{B}.                                  \tag{19}
\]

To prove this, apply (6) with \(a=A\), \(l=pB\). Let
\[
 S=\{i:1\leq i\leq pB,\ p\nmid i\},
\quad
 I=\prod_{i\in S}i,
\quad
 Q=\prod_{i\in S}(Ap+i).
\]
Then
\[
 \binom{p(A+B)}{pB}I=\binom{A+B}{B}Q.                                \tag{20}
\]
The product \(I\) is a unit.

Pair each \(i\in S\) with \(pB-i\). There is no fixed point: if \(2i=pB\), primality and \(p\geq5\) would force \(p\mid i\). Let \(S_1\) contain one member of each pair, chosen by \(2i<pB\). For \(i\in S_1\), set
\[
 d_i=i(pB-i),
 \qquad W=Ap^2(A+B),
 \qquad w_i=W d_i^{-1}.
\]
A direct multiplication gives
\[
 (Ap+i)(Ap+pB-i)=d_i+W.
\]
Therefore
\[
 Q=I P,\qquad P:=\prod_{i\in S_1}(1+w_i).                            \tag{21}
\]

Set
\[
 c=2+v_p(A)+v_p(A+B),
\qquad
 t=3+v_p(A+B)+v_p(B)+v_p(A).
\]
Since \(p^c\mid W\), every \(w_i\) is divisible by \(p^c\). We also claim
\[
 p^{1+v_p(B)}\mid U_1,
 \qquad U_1:=\sum_{i\in S_1}d_i^{-1}.                                \tag{22}
\]
Let \(s=1+v_p(B)\). The interval \([0,pB)\) is a union of blocks of length \(p^s\), so (3) yields
\[
 p^s\mid\sum_{i\in S}i^{-2}.                                       \tag{23}
\]
For every \(i\in S\), since \(p^s\mid pB\),
\[
 \frac1{i(pB-i)}+\frac1{i^2}
 =\frac{pB}{i^2(pB-i)}\equiv0\pmod{p^s}.
\]
Summing and using (23) shows that \(p^s\) divides
\(\sum_{i\in S}d_i^{-1}\). The two members of each complementary pair have the same \(d_i\), so this last sum is \(2U_1\). Since \(2\) is a unit, (22) follows.

It follows that
\[
 \sum_{i\in S_1}w_i=WU_1\equiv0\pmod{p^t}.                           \tag{24}
\]
Moreover, expansion of a finite product shows
\[
 P-1-\sum_iw_i
\]
is a sum of terms containing at least two of the \(w_i\)'s, and hence is divisible by \(p^{2c}\). Condition (18) is exactly what is needed to ensure \(t\leq2c\). Thus (24) gives
\[
 P\equiv1\pmod{p^t}.                                                  \tag{25}
\]

Write \(\widetilde A=\binom{p(A+B)}{pB}\) and
\(\widetilde B=\binom{A+B}{B}\). From (20) and (21),
\[
 (\widetilde A-\widetilde B)I=\widetilde B\,I(P-1).
\]
Now \(p^\gamma\mid\widetilde B\), (25) supplies \(p^t\), and \(I\) is a unit and may be cancelled. This proves (19).

We can remove condition (18) by symmetry. Given \(1\leq j\leq m\), put \(N=m+j\) and
\(\gamma=v_p\binom Nj\). If
\[
 v_p(j)\leq1+v_p(m)+v_p(N),
\]
apply (19) with \((A,B)=(m,j)\). Otherwise the reverse inequality immediately implies
\[
 v_p(m)\leq1+v_p(j)+v_p(N),
\]
so apply (19) with \((A,B)=(j,m)\), then use binomial symmetry. In either case we obtain the refined Jacobsthal congruence
\[
 p^{\gamma+3+v_p(N)+v_p(j)+v_p(m)}
 \mid
 \binom{pN}{pj}-\binom Nj.                                           \tag{26}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. The per-term estimate for indices divisible by \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We first record a valuation inequality. For \(1\leq j\leq m\), with \(N=m+j\) and
\(\gamma=v_p\binom Nj\),
\[
 2v_p(N)\leq v_p(m+2j)+3\gamma+v_p(j).                               \tag{27}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 j\binom Nj=N\binom{N-1}{j-1}
\]
shows
\(v_p(N)\leq v_p(j)+\gamma\). Also
\[
 (m+2j)\binom Nj
 =N\left(\binom{N-1}{j}+2\binom{N-1}{j-1}\right),
\]
so
\(v_p(N)\leq v_p(m+2j)+\gamma\). Adding these two inequalities, and weakening \(2\gamma\) to \(3\gamma\), gives (27).

Let
\[
 X=\binom{pN}{pj},\qquad Y=\binom Nj,
\qquad f=v_p(m).
\]
Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are divisible by \(p^\gamma\): this is clear for \(Y\), and follows for \(X\) from (26). Therefore
\[
 p^{2\gamma}\mid X^2+XY+Y^2.
\]
Combining this with (26) and
\(X^3-Y^3=(X-Y)(X^2+XY+Y^2)\), we get
\[
 v_p(X^3-Y^3)
 \geq3\gamma+3+v_p(N)+v_p(j)+f.                                    \tag{28}
\]
After multiplication by \(m+2j\), inequality (27) implies
\[
 v_p\bigl((m+2j)(X^3-Y^3)\bigr)
 \geq f+3+3v_p(N).                                                    \tag{29}
\]
Equivalently, in the \(p\)-adic integers,
\[
 p^{f+3}N^3\mid(m+2j)(X^3-Y^3).                                     \tag{30}
\]
To justify the factor \(N^3\) exactly, write \(N=p^{v_p(N)}N_0\) with \(p\nmid N_0\); the unit \(N_0^3\) can be inserted into or removed from a divisibility statement.

Now return to \(M\), write
\[
 m=M/p,
 \qquad e=v_p(M)=v_p(m)+1=f+1,
\]
and, for \(0\leq j\leq m\), put
\[
 A_j=\binom{M+pj-1}{M-1}
     =\binom{p(m+j)-1}{pj},
\qquad
 B_j=\binom{m+j-1}{m-1}
     =\binom{m+j-1}{j}.
\]
For \(j\geq1\), the absorption identities
\[
 (m+j)A_j=m\binom{p(m+j)}{pj}=mX,
\qquad
 (m+j)B_j=m\binom{m+j}{j}=mY                                      \tag{31}
\]
give, after cubing and subtracting,
\[
 (m+j)^3(m+2j)(A_j^3-B_j^3)
 =m^3(m+2j)(X^3-Y^3).                                                 \tag{32}
\]
Write \(m=p^fu\) with \(p\nmid u\). By (30), the right side of (32) is divisible by
\[
 p^{3f}\cdot p^{f+3}(m+j)^3=p^{4f+3}(m+j)^3.
\]
Since the \(p\)-adic integers form an integral domain, the nonzero factor \((m+j)^3\) can be cancelled from (32). Hence
\[
 p^{4f+3}=p^{4e-1}
 \mid(m+2j)(A_j^3-B_j^3).                                           \tag{33}
\]
For \(j=0\), the difference is zero. Multiplying (33) by \(p\) and summing over \(0\leq j\leq m\) yields
\[
 p^{4e}\mid
 p\sum_{j=0}^{m}(m+2j)(A_j^3-B_j^3).                                \tag{34}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Proof of the numerator congruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Split \(b(M)\) according as \(p\nmid k\) or \(p\mid k\). Because \(p\mid M\), the latter indices are exactly \(k=pj\), \(0\leq j\leq m=M/p\). For such an index,
\[
 M+2pj=p(m+2j).
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
 b(M)-p\,b(m)
 &=\sum_{\substack{0\leq k\leq M\\p\nmid k}}
      (M+2k)\binom{M+k-1}{M-1}^3\\
 &\quad+p\sum_{j=0}^{m}(m+2j)
 \left[
   \binom{M+pj-1}{M-1}^3
  -\binom{m+j-1}{m-1}^3
 \right].                                                           \tag{35}
\end{aligned}
\]
The first sum is divisible by \(p^{4e}\) by (11), and the second by (34). Thus (1) follows.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Division by the numerator index
--------------------------------------------------------------------

It remains to pass from \(b\) to the sequence itself without losing too much divisibility. First note that \(a(N)\) is indeed integral and has the alternative expression
\[
 A(N):=\sum_{k=0}^{N}
 \left[
 \binom{N+k-1}{N-1}^{3}
 +2\binom{N+k-1}{N}\binom{N+k-1}{N-1}^{2}
 \right].                                                           \tag{36}
\]
The elementary identity
\[
 k\binom{N+k-1}{N-1}=N\binom{N+k-1}{N}
\]
shows term by term that
\[
 (N+2k)\binom{N+k-1}{N-1}^{3}
 =N\left[
 \binom{N+k-1}{N-1}^{3}
 +2\binom{N+k-1}{N}\binom{N+k-1}{N-1}^{2}
 \right].
\]
Hence
\[
 b(N)=N A(N),
\qquad a(N)=A(N).                                                     \tag{37}
\]

Let again \(e=v_p(M)\), and write \(M=p^eu\), \(p\nmid u\). By (37),
\[
 b(M)-p\,b(M/p)
 =M\bigl(A(M)-A(M/p)\bigr).                                         \tag{38}
\]
Combining (1) and (38),
\[
 p^{4e}\mid p^eu\bigl(A(M)-A(M/p)\bigr).
\]
Cancel \(p^e\); since \(u\) is coprime to \(p\), it may also be cancelled. We obtain
\[
 p^{3e}\mid A(M)-A(M/p).                                             \tag{39}
\]

Finally take
\[
 M=np^r,
\qquad n\geq1,
\qquad r\geq1.
\]
Then \(p\mid M\),
\[
 M/p=np^{r-1},
\qquad v_p(M)=v_p(n)+r\geq r.
\]
By (39),
\[
 p^{3v_p(M)}\mid A(np^r)-A(np^{r-1}),

a fortiori
\[
 p^{3r}\mid A(np^r)-A(np^{r-1}).
\]
Using \(A(N)=a(N)\) from (37), this is precisely
\[
 \boxed{\ a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r}}\ }.
\]
This holds for every positive \(n,r\) and every prime \(p\geq5\), as required.
